title: In the mountain pass this side of Sal'
intro: Abd al-Rahman al-Sa'eed introduces this as al-Daymarti's transmission of Abu Tammam's Hamasa, in which a sister's son mourns his uncle Ta'abbata Sharran. Other Hamasa headings give it to Ta'abbata Sharran himself. The genealogist al-Awtabi names al-Shanfara as the nephew, while the commentators al-Marzuqi and al-Tabrizi preferred the later Basran poet and transmitter Khalaf al-Ahmar. The speaker recalls the dead man as both a source of warmth and a feared adversary, then recounts the reckoning with Hudhayl. When he can finally drink again, his wasted body shows what the reckoning has cost.

translation: In the mountain pass this side of Sal'
lies a slain man whose blood will not go unavenged.
1.sharh: The place comes first, then the dead man. What sounds at first like a statement about blood commits the living speaker to answer for a killing.

translation: He left the burden on me and went his way.
For his sake I can carry it.
2.sharh: The burden passes from the dead to the living in the space of a line. Repeating the same word allows the bereaved man to answer the dead man's silent charge.

translation: A sister's son stands ready to avenge him,
fierce in a fight, his knot impossible to undo.
3.sharh: The family relationship itself becomes a guarantee. Al-Marzuqi takes the nephew as the speaker describing himself at a distance. Al-Tabrizi allows another nephew ready to succeed him.

translation: Head lowered, he seeps venom, as a viper bows
its head, a deadly snake breathing poison.
4.sharh: The lowered head might suggest submission until the snake supplies its meaning. The danger gathers almost imperceptibly, like moisture on the skin.

translation: What crushing news has come to us.
It loomed so large that the greatest thing beside it shrank.
5.sharh: The measure of the news is what happens to everything around it. Even a calamity once judged immense seems small beside this death.

translation: Time, ever an oppressor, stripped me
of a proud man whose neighbour suffered no humiliation.
6.sharh: The dead man's refusal of humiliation extended to the people under his protection. Time's theft leaves a whole circle of dependants exposed.

translation: He was sunshine in the bitter cold, and when
Sirius blazed, coolness and shade.
7.sharh: The same host is warmth in one season and shelter from heat in the other. Sirius marks the season when a patch of shade becomes a gift.

translation: Lean at the flanks though never in want,
moist of palm, brave and sure of himself.
8.sharh: Dry flanks and moist hands are deliberately set together. He took little for himself and let others feel the benefit of what he owned.

translation: He travelled with sound judgement, and whenever
he made camp, judgement settled where he settled.
9.sharh: Judgement first seems a traveller's possession. In the second half it acts like a person whose choice of campsite depends on him.

translation: He had two tastes, honey and bitter colocynth,
and all who knew him tasted one or the other.
10.sharh: Friend and enemy knew opposite sides of him firsthand. The taste of honey or colocynth stays in the mouth more vividly than a list of virtues.

translation: In camp, dark-lipped, he walked at ease in trailing robes.
Out raiding he was a lean, swift sim'.
11.sharh: The long robe gives him room for a leisurely gait among his people. On a raid the same man moves with the speed of a lean beast of prey.

translation: A sweeping rain from heavy clouds when he gives,
a lion no one withstands when he strikes.
12.sharh: Cloud and lion describe the reach of his two powers. One spreads benefit over the ground, the other concentrates force in a single adversary.

translation: He rode into terror alone. None
accompanied him but his notched Yemeni blade.
13.sharh: The sword occupies the place in the sentence where a companion ought to stand. The nicks in its edge make it a witness to earlier encounters.

translation: If Hudhayl has blunted his edge,
how often he blunted Hudhayl.
14.sharh: One verb changes hands. What Hudhayl did to one man in killing him is what he had repeatedly done to the tribe's power.

translation: How often he made them kneel on a camping ground
so harsh it wore through a camel's pad.
15.sharh: A kneeling place ought to bring rest at the end of a march. Here the very ground breaks through the camel's natural protection, a measure of Hudhayl's ordeal.

translation: Hudhayl encountered in me a man bold in danger,
who never tires of strife till they do.
16.sharh: The voice of the survivor returns. His claim to endurance makes his opponents' exhaustion the only imaginable end to the quarrel.

translation: He brings the spearhead to drink. Once
it has drunk, he gives it a second draught.
17.sharh: The spear is treated as a thirsty animal led to water. The familiar distinction between first and second drink measures the persistence of the bloodshed.

translation: The hyena laughs over Hudhayl's dead.
You see the wolf raise its voice over them.
18.sharh: Human voices have gone silent. The hyena's apparent laughter and the howl of the wolf fill their place and make the aftermath audible.

translation: The great birds walk with bellies full,
stepping over the men, unable to lift off.
19.sharh: Birds normally wheel above a battlefield. Their awkward walk between bodies shows how much they have eaten.

translation: Young men marched in the midday heat, then travelled
through their night, halting when it lifted.
20.sharh: The narrative goes back to the company on the move. Noon heat and an entire night pass before the first halt at daybreak.

translation: They sipped a few breaths of sleep. As soon as
they nodded off I startled them, and they sprang away.
21.sharh: Counting sleep in mouthfuls makes their rest seem almost too small to swallow. The speaker's cry reaches them at the instant wakefulness gives way.

translation: Each resolute man wore a keen blade about him
like a flash of lightning when drawn.
22.sharh: The same Arabic word means resolute of a man and keen of a sword. The lightning flash makes their shared quickness visible.

translation: We gave Hudhayl the cup of death to drink.
Disgrace, shame and abasement followed it.
23.sharh: “We” replaces the solitary avenger. The cup they pass has an aftertaste that falls on those left alive.

translation: We exacted our blood claim from them. Scarcely
a handful of Lihyan escaped.
24.sharh: Lihyan names the particular branch of Hudhayl caught in the fighting. The event is counted through the few who escaped.

translation: At sunrise it began. When the sun burned hot,
they turned on the spot and fled.
25.sharh: Sunrise and the heat that follows bracket the encounter. The abrupt rush of the last verb makes the retreat feel immediate.

translation: Wine is lawful again. It had been forbidden,
and only with difficulty has it come within reach.
26.sharh: The speaker had bound himself to abstain until the debt of blood was settled. His own vow explains why the cup can be passed now.

translation: Pour it for me, Sawad son of Amr.
Since my uncle's death my body has wasted to a stick.
27.sharh: The public reckoning ends in a request to one companion. The drink can be restored at once, but the survivor's thin body still bears the loss.

1.1.2.head: الشِّعب
1.1.2.meaning: A pass or cleft between mountains.

1.1.5.head: سَلع
1.1.5.meaning: Sal', a hill at Medina. The location figures in the old discussion of authorship.

1.2.4.head: طُلَّ
1.2.4.meaning: Of blood, to be shed without the killing being answered for.

2.1.2.head: العِبء
2.1.2.meaning: A weight to carry, here the duty left by a slain relative.

2.2.4.head: مُستَقِلّ
2.2.4.meaning: Able to lift and bear a load.

3.2.1.head: مَصِع
3.2.1.meaning: Formidable and steady in a fight.

3.2.2.head: عُقدَة
3.2.2.meaning: A knot, figuratively the fixed resolution binding him.

5.1.4.head: مُصمَئِلّ
5.1.4.meaning: Crushing or overwhelming, said of a calamity.

5.2.5.head: الأَجَلّ
5.2.5.meaning: The greatest or most momentous thing.

6.1.1.head: بَزَّ
6.1.1.meaning: Stripped me of something dear by force.

6.2.1.head: أَبِيّ
6.2.1.meaning: Proud and unwilling to accept humiliation.

7.2.2.meaning: Al-Shi'ra, Sirius, whose rising was associated with summer heat.

8.2.4.head: مُدِلّ
8.2.4.meaning: Assured of his own courage and worth.

10.1.3.head: أَري
10.1.3.meaning: Honey, the sweet side of his character.

10.1.4.head: شَري
10.1.4.meaning: Colocynth, a plant proverbial for its intense bitterness.

11.1.4.meaning: Dark-lipped, a feature al-Tabrizi says was admired. Al-Farisi takes the word to describe his brown complexion.

11.1.5.head: رِفَلّ
11.1.5.meaning: One who lets a long robe trail as he walks.

11.2.3.head: سِمع
11.2.3.meaning: Sim', a swift beast traditionally described as the offspring of a wolf and a hyena.

11.2.4.head: أَزَلّ
11.2.4.meaning: Lean in the hindquarters and fleet.

13.2.3-4.head: اليَماني الأَفَلّ
13.2.3-4.meaning: “The notched Yemeni.” A sword of Yemeni make whose edge shows wear.

14.1.4.head: شَبا
14.1.4.meaning: Its cutting edge, standing for a man's force.

15.2.1.head: جَعجَع
15.2.1.meaning: Hard, inhospitable ground for a halt.

15.2.4.head: الأَظَلّ
15.2.4.meaning: The underside of a camel's foot.

16.1.1.head: صَلِيَ
16.1.1.meaning: Encountered or suffered, literally felt the heat of a fire.

16.1.4.head: خِرق
16.1.4.meaning: A man bold enough to face a perilous undertaking.

17.1.2.head: الأَلَّة
17.1.2.meaning: A spear or its bright head.

17.2.5.head: عَلّ
17.2.5.meaning: A second drink after the first watering.

18.2.4.head: اِستَهَلَّ
18.2.4.meaning: Raise the voice, here of a wolf howling.

19.1.4.head: بِطان
19.1.4.meaning: Gorged, heavy with a full belly.

19.2.3.head: اِستَقَلَّ
19.2.3.meaning: Rise clear of the ground under one's own power.

20.1.1.head: فُتُوّ
20.1.1.meaning: A company of young men introduced by an Arabic construction recalling an exploit.

20.2.4.meaning: Lifted or cleared away, of the night.

21.2.1.head: هَوَّمَ
21.2.1.meaning: Began to nod off. Al-Marzuqi and al-Farisi give “grew intoxicated”, carrying on the image of drinking sleep.

21.2.3.head: اِشمَعَلَّ
21.2.3.meaning: Sprang up and moved off briskly.

22.1.5.head: ماضٍ
22.1.5.meaning: A keen blade. The same word has just described a man firm in purpose.

25.2.4.head: اِجفَأَلَّ
25.2.4.meaning: Broke into a headlong retreat. The electronic transcripts suggest the shorter ajfalu. Al-Farisi’s longer form supplies the rhythm of this foot.

26.2.1.head: لَأي
26.2.1.meaning: With difficulty and after a long delay.

27.1.3-5.head: سَواد اِبن عَمرٍو
27.1.3-5.meaning: Sawad ibn Amr, the companion addressed when the speaker asks for wine.

19.1.3.head: مَشى
19.1.3.meaning: Walk on their feet, too full to rise. Al-Farisi and al-Marzuqi have “flutter” and al-Tabrizi has “go out in the morning”.

23.1.1.head: سَقى
23.1.1.meaning: Made them drink from the cup of death. Al-Awtabi has “we brought it to them in the morning”.

3.1.4-5.head: اِبنُ أُخت
3.1.4-5.meaning: “A sister’s son.” Al-Marzuqi hears the speaker naming his own relationship to the dead man. Al-Tabrizi also allows a second nephew who would inherit the duty from him.

14.1.3.head: هُذَيل
14.1.3.meaning: Hudhayl, the tribe the nephew holds answerable for his uncle’s death. In recounting the reprisal he singles out one of its branches, Lihyan.
